title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All planned pairs completed (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We present the preregistered design, execution accounting, a prominent disclosure of a labeled reproducibility gap in the Mininet holdout selection, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating natural‑language intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational gains but raises safety risks: incorrect sequences can violate workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must‑be‑down-for) and cause outages. Prior work therefore proposes grounding and verifier‑assisted repair (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. However, the marginal operational value of GVR depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompting policy, (ii) validator coverage, and (iii) the permitted repair budget and repair effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: for a fixed generator output per task, does invoking a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair call (if needed) reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to applying the generator output unchecked? We executed a paired design that shares the same deterministic initial candidate across conditions to isolate the marginal effect of validation+repair on that candidate.
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies document LLM factual errors, hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; mitigation approaches include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and guarded agent architectures. NetOps prototypes show feasibility of intent→configuration generation but rarely provide instrumented, preregistered failure‑rate measurements in production‑like settings. Architectural proposals recommend combining LLM generation with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checkers) and with bounded agent patterns; red‑team audits document configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can alter safety outcomes. Our work contributes an externally auditable, preregistered paired measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic validation+repair on identical generator outputs, thereby clarifying when GVR can provide measurable validator‑detected safety gains.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The preregistered study (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design (n = 200 tasks), a shared deterministic initial generation per task, and at most one automated repair prompt per task. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the prespecified test is an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The analysis executor was paired_binary_analysis_v1.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank (200 tasks; four topology clusters of 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial/final states, workflow constraints, and required sequences. The primary deterministic checker enforces syntactic and intent/constraint rules and yields structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator blind spots.

Adapter semantics and determinism reconciliation. The execution contract required shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single initial candidate is produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions to obtain a controlled paired contrast. The archived model configuration lists the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and contains an explicit field for sampling parameters; that field is null in the archived configuration. Determinism at runtime was achieved by adapter enforcement of the shared_initial generation policy rather than by relying on an explicit non‑null temperature parameter. The execution accounting artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, which demonstrate that exactly one hosted generation was produced per task and reused across both conditions. These adapter‑enforced semantics are therefore the operational mechanism by which the run achieved deterministic shared‑initial sampling despite the configuration's explicit sampling field being null.

Repair policy, budgeting, and contamination handling. If the primary validator reported violations, the preregistered policy allowed a single automated repair prompt to the same LLM and re‑validation of the repaired candidate. The adapter enforced a global model‑call cap (maximum_model_calls = 400). The contamination plan excluded pairs from primary analysis if Batfish‑style validator verdicts disagreed with Mininet emulator results on the randomized 10% holdout; such exclusions were to be deterministic and preregistered. We note and prominently report below a labeled reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized seed used to select the Mininet 10% holdout is not present in the labeled artifacts, which prevents exact bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of which tasks comprised that holdout and therefore limits deterministic replay of the contamination check selection.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), repair_calls_used = 0, maximum_model_calls = 400. Adapter/provider accounting reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and no failed provider calls.

Primary outcomes. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% under the chosen generator/prompting and shared_initial policy, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis (≥50% relative reduction) could not be meaningfully evaluated on this sample.

Secondary checks and repair statistics. No validator failures occurred; consequently the repair branch was never invoked and the preregistered secondary estimands (repair‑iteration distribution, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) have no empirical data in this run. The preregistered Mininet holdout contamination check (20 tasks) recorded zero validator–emulator disagreements in the contamination summary; however, as noted above, the labeled artifact set does not contain the explicit seed that deterministically identifies which tasks were in that holdout, which limits exact deterministic reconstruction of that specific holdout draw.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The null result (no validator‑detected failures) is an artifact‑grounded empirical outcome for this curated task bank and the chosen deterministic shared‑initial generation policy. It does not imply that GVR is universally unhelpful: GVR's marginal value depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and on validator coverage. In this run the generator+prompt policy produced outputs that satisfied the machine‑checkable task constraints for every sampled task, leaving no validator‑detectable failures for GVR to correct.

Method design tradeoffs. The shared_initial paired design isolates the incremental effect of validation+repair on an identical generator output by removing sampling variance across conditions. That internal control comes at the cost of excluding gains obtainable by re‑sampling the LLM (e.g., generating alternative candidate draws that might fail or succeed). For practitioners interested in unconditional operational failure risk, a mixed design with independent multi‑sample draws per condition would better estimate unconditional failure prevalence and repair coverage.

Validator fidelity and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators codify a finite set of checks; emulation or device testing remains necessary to surface validator blind spots. The Mininet holdout produced zero disagreements in the recorded summary, but the missing labeled selection seed prevents deterministic replay of that particular holdout selection and therefore constrains the evidentiary strength of the contamination check. We therefore recommend larger, seed‑recorded holdouts and multiple emulator types when assessing validator completeness.

Operational implications. Before committing operational resources to automated repair, practitioners should (1) measure baseline validator failure prevalence for the intended generator/prompt policy, (2) expand validator fidelity where failures are rare but production risk remains, and (3) consider multi‑sample generation or larger repair budgets when baseline failures are nontrivial. When baseline failures are rare under a production generator policy, a low‑budget single‑repair GVR yields limited marginal validator‑detected benefit.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The artifact‑grounded result underscores that GVR’s marginal measured value is workload‑dependent: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under the production generator/prompt policy, a low‑budget repair mechanism provides no measured validator‑detected benefit. Future preregistered studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, increase repair budgets, record holdout selection seeds, and evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies to fully characterize practical operational gains.

Reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of that specific holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements. limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
